title: Only the melt can answer
topic: Texas A&M announced a $2 million grant for the Aggie AI Foundry, a planned lab where AI proposes alloys and robotic arms mix, melt and test them, and its own researcher says no computer tool can predict an alloy

requests.purpose: Give the film one recognizable robotic arm and sample line that changes state through the film: it takes element vials into a crucible, sets the crucible in a glowing furnace, carries the sample to a test rig, loads and bends the real metal, and at the close tips the melt into a mold, so the planned Aggie AI Foundry action is a drawn object a viewer can follow.
requests.prompt: Author an original finished React and SVG object in the current Remotion engine. A generic multi-axis robotic arm with a rounded warm gray shell, a visible wrist joint and a two finger gripper holding tongs, no brand marks. Beside it a rack of glass element vials, a ceramic crucible, a furnace opening that glows amber with a heat shimmer, and a sample test rig with a clamp and a needle gauge. Soft key light from the upper left through a lab window, cool fill from the right, contact shadows on a worn steel line bed, scuffed paint and a slightly leaning sample tray so nothing is symmetric. A disclosed illustration of a planned lab, never a real arm, furnace, rig or Texas A&M building.
requests.source_limit: Disclosed illustration of a planned automated alloy line. Not an existing Texas A&M facility, not a named arm or furnace model, not a real melting method, and the test shows no measured result.

requests.purpose: Give the arm its world and its records: a periodic table wall display with tiles that light, a mesh of mixes, a stream of recipe cards and a pile over a bench edge, a news release card with a dateline stamp and a $2 million tag, a planned foundry bay outline, an AI panel writing a recipe card, a quote card with a prediction gauge that fills partway and stops, calendar month pages and a one-week strip, a goal stamp, a not a result tag and a blank opening date field.

A generic metals lab wall with a window onto post oak woods and grass, a periodic table display whose tiles light amber, a fine mesh of lines between lit tiles, hand-sized recipe cards with ruled lines, a worn bench with a rolling pencil, a plain news release card with a crooked rubber dateline stamp and a paper tag, a pencil outline of a foundry bay with a PLANNED stamp, a flat AI panel with a recipe card, a quote card with a pen signature line, a prediction gauge with a needle, a stack of wall calendar pages, a seven cell week strip, a GOAL stamp, a not a result tag and a blank form field with a dash. Maintained but worn, nothing symmetric, warm paper against cool gray steel. No logos, no university marks, no brand marks.

story_contract.opening_question: How do you find one good alloy among a trillion possible mixes?
story_contract.actor: Texas A&M University Department of Materials Science and Engineering, which announced a $2 million WoodNext Foundation grant
story_contract.action: Announced a grant to build the Aggie AI Foundry, a planned lab where AI proposes alloys and computer-controlled robotic arms mix, melt and test them.
story_contract.change: Alloy development would move toward an automated line where AI proposes and robotic arms make and test the metal, with a goal of a week or less instead of months.
story_contract.affected_people: Materials scientists and students at Texas A&M. No person is named beyond the quoted researcher.
story_contract.consequence: The metal still has to be made and tested, because a computer can predict some behavior but no computer tool can predict an alloy.
story_contract.source_limit: Every verb about the facility is future tense. The release gives no opening date, building, melting method or measured result, and a week or less is the university's goal.
story_contract.closing_answer: The AI can suggest, and only the melt can answer.

scenes.advances: Several dozen tiles of the periodic table light one after another on the lab wall. Lines weave between the lit tiles into a dense mesh of possible mixes. A tag reading roughly a trillion ways settles on the mesh while one candidate point glows.

Recipe cards fall in a steady stream from the mesh toward a lab bench. The cards pile over the bench edge and a pencil rolls off. A gloved hand sorts one card into a tray, reaches again, and stops as the cards bury the tray.

A news release card slides onto the desk and its headline writes in. A dateline stamp reading Oct. 22, 2026 lands crooked on the card. A tag reading $2 million grant attaches beside the headline. An outline of a planned foundry bay draws in beside the card and takes a PLANNED stamp.

The AI panel writes a candidate alloy recipe card and sends it down the line. The robotic arm takes element vials from the rack and drops them into a crucible to mix. The arm sets the crucible in the furnace and the metal glows amber. The arm carries the sample to the test rig and the rig clamps it.

A quote card slides in and the name Raymundo Arróyave writes under his quoted words. On the panel the computer's prediction gauge fills partway and a tag reading some behavior marks the level. Over the clamped sample on the rig the same gauge stays empty and a question mark appears.
The clamped sample cools from amber to gray while the arm waits parked clear of the rig. The ram comes down and loads the clamped sample. The sample bends under the ram and the needle gauge swings.
Calendar month pages flip away one after another. A one-week strip slides in and its day cells fill. A tag reading goal lands on the week strip.

A GOAL stamp lands crooked on the week strip. A tag reading not a result attaches to the stamp. The release card returns with an opening date field clipped to it, and the field stays blank with a dash.

A new recipe card with new swatches writes on the panel and glows once, while the rig sets the bent bar aside and a mold slides onto the anvils. The arm tips the crucible and the amber melt pours into the mold until it is full. The new recipe card dims and the arm sets the crucible upright while the full mold holds its glow on the test rig.

art_direction.palette_reason: Warm paper carries the records, cool slate steel holds the line, post oak green sits outside the window, the pale shell is the one clean value and a single amber is kept for the melt, the lit tiles and the goal stamp.
art_direction.shape_language: A rounded arm shell against rectangular steel benches, boxy furnace and rig, and flat paper cards with worn corners. Nothing is symmetric: the tray leans, the stamp lands crooked, the pencil rolls off.

lighting.motivation: Soft window light from the upper left warms the bench and the paper, cool fill from the right shades the steel, and the amber melt throws its own warm light on the arm.

hero.silhouette: A rounded multi-axis robotic arm with a two finger gripper beside a crucible furnace and a clamp test rig on a worn steel line.
hero.finish: Lit upper-left shell with a soft highlight, cool shaded right side, scuffed paint, a furnace opening glowing amber with a heat shimmer, a needle gauge and soft contact shadows on worn steel.

art_direction.focal_hierarchy: The arm or the glowing melt first, the recipe card or the gauge second, the tags and stamps third, the lab wall and window last.
art_direction.motion_language: The arm moves with continuous acceleration and braking, cards slide and settle without bounce, stamps land once, the gauge needle swings and settles, and the camera holds while objects perform.

signature_shot.reason: The arm tips the crucible and the amber melt fills the mold on the test rig, the answer in one movement.

captions.text: Several dozen elements can be mixed in roughly a trillion ways.
No person can sort through that many.
Texas A&M announced a two million dollar grant,
to build the Aggie AI Foundry.
The plan is that AI proposes alloys,
and computer-controlled robotic arms mix, melt and test them.
Raymundo Arróyave says a computer can predict some behavior,
but no computer tool anywhere can predict an alloy's behavior.
So the work has to be done on the actual metal.
The goal is developing alloys in a week or less, not months.
That is the university's goal, not a result.
The release gives no opening date.
